extracted.intended_audience: newspaper reporters and journalists covering speeches
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reporters on covering spoken addresses and converting them into newspaper stories—includes note-taking, use of advance copies/translators, lead selection, structure, and quotation/paraphrase practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use liaison/translator for non-English speeches
rubrics_metrics.description: If a speaker's talk is in another language, arrive early to find someone to translate or have an official delegate someone to sit with the reporter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a translator sits with the reporter they may converse more freely; when using a second-hand translation, put the speech largely in paraphrase rather than direct quotation because multiple translations produce different shades of meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Note audience reactions and get summaries when language is an obstacle
rubrics_metrics.description: If unable to understand the language, take notes on times the audience reacted most vigorously and afterwards ask an intelligent listener to summarize the high spots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not knowing the language doesn't mean not getting the story; resourcefulness can make up for language barriers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview speaker immediately after speech to verify quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever possible the reporter interviews the speaker immediately after the talk and verifies the quotations and paraphrases he intends to use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the reporter's chief protection if a story brings a complaint of misquotation and shows the city editor the reporter went the limit to ensure accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely solely on abstracts or advance copies
rubrics_metrics.description: An abstract or an advance copy is an assistance but is no substitute for listening; an advance copy does not excuse the reporter from attending the lecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speakers may tone down abstracts, omit strong passages at delivery, change talks between audiences, or fail to arrive—so attend, listen, and verify rather than assuming the advance copy equals the delivered speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Converting a faithful advance copy into a story
rubrics_metrics.description: When an advance copy faithfully represents the delivered speech, the reporter can convert it into a story quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Process: skim the manuscript and check printable passages in the margin, cut out checked passages and paste them into desired sequence, rewrite long passages from direct quotation into briefer paraphrase if needed, then write a lead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taking serviceable notes: full sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Put the notes into full sentences rather than nounless or verbless half-phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full sentences aid accurate listening and later transcription; avoid terse fragments that lose sense out of context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taking serviceable notes: create interest to stay attentive
rubrics_metrics.description: Create an interest in the speech as an aid to unflagging and accurate listening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintaining reporter interest helps avoid haphazard listening that dilutes the subsequent story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taking serviceable notes: learn speaker's oratorical trademarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Become familiar with the speaker's oratorical trademarks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge of a speaker's typical phrases, inflections, and gestures aids recognizing and accurately recording important statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taking serviceable notes: verify quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify quotations as part of taking serviceable notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checking quotes with the speaker (when possible) and being careful while selecting quotes protects against misquotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensing a speech while preserving impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Compress a long speech (e.g., 5,400 words) into a short account (e.g., 450 words) selected so that it makes upon readers the same impact as the speech did on listeners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Condensing requires skillful selection; avoid arbitrary cuts—choose material that preserves the original impact and balance fairness to the speaker with reader interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain individuality in speech stories
rubrics_metrics.description: A speech story must reflect one particular speech and avoid being too much like other speech stories the paper has carried.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use variety—especially in the lead—and the full flexibility of rhetoric to manifest the reporter's individual skill and prevent monotony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance fairness/accuracy against interestingness
rubrics_metrics.description: The reporter balances two desires: to be fair and accurate to the speaker and to be interesting to readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not omit speaker's qualifying words (probably/possibly) purely to make the story punchier; integrity compels inclusion even if it weakens immediate impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a lead type appropriately (five main categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are five categories of leads for speech stories that a reporter can use to avoid uniform openings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The categories are direct-quotation leads, name leads, conditions leads, modified-quotation/paraphrase leads, and participial/tie-in leads; choose based on what best captures the story's dominant angle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct-quotation lead — single-sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: A single sentence of quotation is useful when one statement or idea outweighs all else in the speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The quoted sentence should be reasonably short—avoid complex sentences with many subordinate clauses ('hell divers') that are hard to encompass at a glance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct-quotation lead — full-paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an entire paragraph of quotation when the most compelling idea is too intricate for a single sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some papers require the speaker's name in the first paragraph when using this form; full-paragraph quotations can deaden interest if overused but are serviceable and should not be shunned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct-quotation lead — catchword/slogan
rubrics_metrics.description: When a speech is built around frequent repetition of one vivid idea, use a short slogan lead (a catchword) to grab readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slogan leads must be short, crackling, and rely on surprise or provocation; they are powerful but risky and cannot be used frequently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Name lead — speaker's name
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the name lead when 'what was said' is not the best part of the story and the speaker is so generally known that the name itself is impressive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid this form if the speaker made powerful statements; use it sparingly as it can be dull and redundant if repeated (e.g., also used in advance notices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Name lead — subject of the speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead with the subject when the topic is unusual, currently of high interest, or automatically provocative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This form is useful as relief from other lead types but is too weak for addresses where 'what was said' would make strong copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Name lead — title of the speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the speech's title as a lead when the title itself is catchy or stimulating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a variation appropriate for relief purposes, yawny talks, or mediocre addresses by less-known speakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions (tie-in) lead
rubrics_metrics.description: Hook the speech immediately into the background or circumstances from which it grows (conditions under which the address was given).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sparingly and only when the linking of conditions and the speech is completely natural; forced linkage fails and makes a weak lead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modified-quotation (paraphrase) lead — 'old faithful'
rubrics_metrics.description: A paraphrase lead gives a lot of information in small space and proclaims 'Plenty of substance in this story.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It may summarize principal topics with 'that' clauses—avoid more than three 'that' clauses and avoid an interior 'that' that muddies grammar; the two-'that' and single-idea variants are useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participial/tie-in lead
rubrics_metrics.description: A participial lead ties the speech directly into relevant background or recent news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective when speeches are outgrowths of earlier news; watch for lost or nonparallel participles that can confuse readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow up the lead — elaborate and buttress
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not omit elaboration of the material used in the lead; the body must expand and explain what the lead promised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the lead topic received little attention from the speaker, say so to keep it in context; if lead used a single statement, buttress other major declarations to give the story structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggested block structure for speech stories (short form)
rubrics_metrics.description: A good structure for typical speech stories organizes material into blocks: lead block, summary of other important statements, catch-all, elaboration of lead, expansion of other topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use: First block — lead angle; Second — summary of other important statements; Third — catch-all; Fourth — expand lead; Fifth — expand other topics in order mentioned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associated Press structure for very long speech accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: For very long speeches (more than a column) use the AP seven-block structure to facilitate later trimming by editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blocks: 1) lead topic, 2) summary of next best statements, 3) catch-all, 4) two- or three-paragraph abstract of lead topic, 5) several-paragraph abstract of topics in block 2, 6) further expansion of lead topic, 7) further expansion of second block; reserve for mile-long stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of reporter influence: direct quotation selection risks distortion
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct quotation still makes the reporter a factor because rarely are all speaker's words given; in plucking quotes a careless reporter can distort as much as by rewriting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select direct quotations so that despite condensing they remain in focus and in context—snatches here and there risk changing the speaker's intended impact (example with Mr. Foster).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect quotation: uses and advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect quotation presents the speaker's ideas mainly in his own words but altered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: permits modest condensing, untangles intricate sentences and smooths grammar, and covers parts the reporter failed to gather precisely enough for direct quotation; keep context in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paraphrase: when and why to use it
rubrics_metrics.description: Paraphrase uses the reporter's own words rather than the speaker's, allowing more thorough abbreviating and repair of broken diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paraphrasing compensates for lost gesture and inflection by choosing words that have the same net effect on readers as the speaker's original speech; reporters should not hesitate to paraphrase to obtain accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: What qualifies as an acceptable direct quotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct quotation does not demand literal reproduction if it nevertheless conveys the substance, spirit, and typical language of the remark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A quotation may be 'direct' if it: 1) conveys the substance of the remark in full accuracy, 2) conveys the spirit in which it was made, and 3) uses language typical of the speaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid repeating identical lead forms across related coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use the same weak lead (e.g., a name lead) if an earlier advance story used the same form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeat use of identical lead types across advance notices and later accounts makes coverage feel familiar and listless and will lose readers' interest.
